mercy_translation.text:
These things are said to those outside who heap up arguments for themselves. But if someone from among us asks, not out of contentiousness but from a desire to learn, why he endured the cross rather than another kind of death, let that person hear that no other way would have benefited us as this did, and that the Lord fittingly endured it for our sake.

For if he came himself to bear the curse that had come upon us, how else could he become a curse except by receiving the death appointed under a curse? This is the cross, for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree.”

Again, if the death of the Lord is the ransom of all, and by his death “the dividing wall of hostility” is broken down and the calling of the nations takes place, how could he have called us if he had not been crucified? For only upon the cross does one die with hands outstretched. Therefore it was fitting for the Lord to endure this and stretch out his hands, so that with one he might draw the ancient people and with the other those from the nations, joining both together in himself.

He himself also said this, indicating by what kind of death he was going to ransom all: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all to myself.”

Again, if the devil, the enemy of our race, having fallen from heaven, wanders in the lower air and there rules over demons like himself in disobedience, working illusions through them upon those who are deceived and trying to hinder those ascending—and concerning him the Apostle says, “according to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience”—while the Lord came to cast down the devil, cleanse the air, and prepare for us the way of ascent into heaven, as the Apostle said, “through the veil, that is, his flesh,” and this had to happen through death: by what other death could these things have happened except the one accomplished in the air, namely the cross? For only the one who is perfected on the cross dies suspended in the air. Therefore the Lord fittingly endured this death.

For being lifted up in this way, he cleansed the air from the devil's plotting and from every attack of demons, saying, “I saw Satan fall like lightning.” And he renewed and opened the ascent into heaven, saying again, “Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates.” It was not the Word himself who needed the gates opened, for he is Lord of all, nor was any created thing closed to its Maker. We were the ones who needed this, whom he carried upward through his own body. For just as he offered it to death on behalf of all, so through it he also prepared the way of ascent into heaven.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius gives several symbolic and theological reasons for the cross: curse-bearing, gathering Jew and Gentile, defeat of hostile powers, and opening the way to heaven.
The cosmological language concerning the air reflects the biblical and late-antique conceptual world of the text.
